title: State budgets can keep growing while using targeted adjustments and prior surplus
source_unit: National Association of State Budget Officers Spring 2026 Fiscal Survey of States; state budget offices
geography: United States; states, territories, and District of Columbia budget-office survey, with state counts reported for selected items

observations.period: Fiscal 2027 proposed budgets compared with estimated fiscal 2026

denominator.unit: US state budget offices represented in the survey context

median_general_fund_spending_change.unit: percent change in proposed fiscal 2027 general-fund spending from estimated fiscal 2026

observations.method: NASBO summary of data gathered from state budget offices; spring survey describes governors' proposed budgets and fiscal conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The spending figure is a median proposal comparison, not enacted implementation. The adjustment counts do not identify the affected agency, program, place, worker, or household.
observations.subgroup: States reporting selected budget adjustment strategies; the survey summary does not provide a common service-level denominator for these counts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Targeted cuts and vacant-position reductions can coexist with protected or expanded priority services; revenue increases and one-time spending can change the mix without reducing total nominal spending.

observations.period: Fiscal 2026 revenue compared with original forecasts

denominator.unit: states reporting revenue status in the NASBO summary

observations.method: NASBO state budget-office report of fiscal 2026 revenue relative to original forecasts at the time of data collection.
observations.uncertainty: The classification is a fiscal forecast comparison, not a measure of household income, service affordability, or final year-end revenue for every state.
observations.subgroup: States classified by reported revenue performance relative to original forecast.
observations.counterinterpretation: Revenue above forecast can coexist with unmet needs, restricted balances, or service cuts; revenue below forecast can be absorbed by reserves, federal funds, borrowing, or reprioritization.

denominator.unit: US states in the survey context

rainy_day_balances.value: most states projected to maintain or increase balances in dollars

median_balance_share.value: projected to tick down slightly as spending grows faster than reserves

total_balances.value: projected to decline as prior surplus funds are spent, while remaining above pre-pandemic historical highs
total_balances.unit: rainy day funds plus general-fund ending balances

observations.method: NASBO summary of state rainy-day and general-fund ending-balance projections.
observations.uncertainty: Balance availability differs by law, earmark, fiscal calendar, and political decision; the summary does not identify which programs receive or lose funds.
observations.subgroup: States with different reserve rules, spending needs, and revenue bases.
observations.counterinterpretation: Spending down prior surplus can fund planned one-time investments rather than indicate immediate fiscal distress or service failure.

related_sources.claim: Pew Fiscal 50 supplies a state-by-state reserve-capacity comparator and reports fiscal 2025 operating-day measures.

boundary: This record measures state-budget capacity and proposed adjustment strategies. It does not establish enacted implementation, service quality, household or firm incidence, local-government capacity, political trust, or geopolitical leverage. The next test is a named state service or shock followed through implementation and lived outcome.
